blocks.text: By the early 1960s, government computers were taking on calculations generated by surveying, mapping, geodesy and engineering. Field observations or map measurements went in; adjusted coordinates, reduced observations and tables came back. Surveyors still plotted and interpreted those results on paper. The computer had become part of the mapping workflow before anyone could call up a digital map.

blocks.text: A programme could transform a trig station’s coordinates without knowing the station’s name, its role in the network or which features depended on it. The machine applied the method; staff kept the geographic meaning in field books, card decks and office procedures.

blocks.text: The word “computer” needs care in this period. In the Department of Lands and Survey, computers were staff whose job was calculation. Russell Gladstone Dick’s 1966 account describes office computers helping maintain survey records, alongside the newer use of electronic machines for demanding mathematics.
